lesson.title: Why One Subject Is Never Enough: The Role of Replication
lesson.summary: Replication means applying each treatment to enough experimental units that chance variation among individuals averages out, letting real treatment effects stand out from random noise.
lesson.body:
Replication in an experiment means applying each treatment to more than one experimental unit, so that chance differences between individuals do not masquerade as a treatment effect. It is a different idea from repeating an entire experiment on a different day or in a different lab, which is sometimes called replicating a study; here replication refers to having enough units within a single experiment's treatment groups. If a researcher gives a new headache medication to exactly one patient and a placebo to exactly one other patient, and the medicated patient feels better, there is no way to know whether the drug worked or whether that particular patient simply would have felt better anyway, since headaches come and go for all sorts of reasons.

The statistical reason replication matters comes down to variability. Every individual, plant, or manufactured item differs somewhat from every other one, even before any treatment is applied, simply due to natural variation. When a treatment is given to only one unit, the researcher cannot separate the effect of the treatment from this ordinary individual variability. But when a treatment is given to, say, 25 units, the individual quirks tend to average out, and the group's average response becomes a much more stable, trustworthy estimate of what the treatment truly does. This is the same logic behind the law of large numbers: averages computed from more observations vary less from sample to sample than averages computed from few observations.

Consider a worked example. A company wants to know whether a new packaging design increases the shelf life of bread. If it tests the new packaging on 5 loaves and the old packaging on 5 loaves, and finds an average shelf life of 9 days for the new design versus 7 days for the old one, that 2 day difference is suggestive, but with only 5 loaves per group, a couple of unusually mold-resistant loaves could easily explain the gap. If the company instead tests 100 loaves per condition and still finds a 2 day average difference, that same 2 day gap is far more convincing, because it is much less plausible that random loaf-to-loaf variation alone produced it across 100 independent loaves rather than 5.

Replication also makes it possible to estimate how much chance variation to expect, which is essential for any later hypothesis test or confidence interval. With only one unit per treatment, there is no way to compute a standard deviation within a group at all, since a single number has no spread of its own. With multiple units per treatment, the researcher can calculate how much responses vary among units receiving the identical treatment, and that internal spread becomes the yardstick against which the difference between treatment groups is judged. A large treatment effect relative to that natural spread suggests a real effect; a difference no bigger than the ordinary within-group scatter suggests the result could easily be due to chance alone.

Replication works hand in hand with random assignment. Random assignment ensures that the units within each treatment group are, on average, comparable to the units in other groups before treatment; replication then ensures there are enough units in each group for that averaging-out process to happen reliably. A design with only 2 units per treatment technically uses random assignment correctly, but it has so little replication that its conclusions rest on a shaky statistical foundation, which is why real experiments almost always involve dozens, hundreds, or more experimental units per treatment group.
